name: Telugu

script.overview:
Telugu script is an **abugida** descended from Brahmi, written left to right, closely related to the Kannada script. Each consonant letter carries an inherent short *a*: క is *ka*. To give a consonant a different vowel you attach a **vowel sign** (called *gunintham*): కా kā, కి ki, కు ku, కె ke, కో kō. Vowel letters (అ ఆ ఇ ...) are used only at the start of a syllable.

Most consonants have a small tick on top called the **talakaṭṭu** (తలకట్టు, ‘head-tie’). When a vowel sign is added, the tick is often replaced by the sign itself, so learn each consonant together with its vowel-sign forms; the shapes are rounded, built from circles and hooks.

To show a consonant with no vowel, Telugu uses the **pollu** (virama ్): క్ is a bare *k*. In everyday writing, though, a vowelless consonant usually joins the next one as a **vottu** (వత్తు, subjoined form) written below or beside it: క + క = క్క (kka), స + త = స్త (sta), ప + ర = ప్ర (pra). Learning about twenty common vottulu covers almost everything you will read.

Other marks: ం (*sunna*, anusvara) is a nasal, pronounced *m* at the end of a word and as the matching nasal before a consonant; ః (visarga) appears in a few Sanskrit words; ఁ (*arasunna*, half-nasal) and the letter ఱ belong to older spelling and are no longer pronounced differently. Telugu has its own digits (౦ ౧ ౨ ...), though Western digits are what you will see almost everywhere today.

where: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana (India), with large communities in Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, Odisha and the diaspora (USA, Gulf, UK)
tagline: The most widely spoken Dravidian language, with a melodious, vowel-final sound and a booming film and tech culture.
intro:
**Telugu** (తెలుగు) is a Dravidian language, a relative of Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam, spoken by close to a hundred million people. Because almost every word ends in a vowel, its sound is often compared to Italian, and early European visitors called it *the Italian of the East*. It is the language of Tollywood, one of India's largest film industries, and of the tech hubs of Hyderabad.

Grammatically Telugu is **agglutinative**: meaning is built by stacking suffixes onto a stem. *ఇల్లు* (illu, house) becomes *ఇంట్లో* (iṇṭlō, in the house) and *ఇంటికి* (iṇṭiki, to the house). Verbs carry endings for person, number and gender, so the subject pronoun is often dropped: *వస్తాను* (vastānu) alone means *I will come*. The basic word order is subject–object–verb, and there is no ergative construction.

The vocabulary mixes native Dravidian words with a large layer of Sanskrit and, in everyday speech, many English and (especially in Hyderabad) Urdu words. Telugu has a clear **formal/informal** divide: *మీరు* (mīru) is the polite or plural *you*, *నువ్వు* (nuvvu) the intimate one, and verbs agree with that choice.

This course teaches the **standard modern spoken language** heard in Telugu media, based on the coastal and Hyderabad varieties. Where written forms and everyday speech differ (e.g. *ఏమిటి* vs colloquial *ఏంటి*, ēmiṭi vs ēṇṭi) the notes tell you which is which.
romanizationNote: The romanization shows how words are actually pronounced. A macron marks a long vowel: Telugu contrasts short *e/o* with long *ē/ō* (మెడ meḍa neck vs మేడ mēḍa upstairs), so pay attention to it. A dot under a letter marks a retroflex sound made with the tongue curled back (ṭ ḍ ṇ ḷ); plain t d n l are dental, with the tongue touching the teeth. Doubled letters (kk, tt, ḷḷ) are genuinely held longer. *ch* and *j* are as in English, but in many words before a, o, u a lot of speakers say *ts* and *dz* (చాలా chālā is often tsālā). The anusvara ం is written *m* at the end of a word (పుస్తకం pustakam) and as the matching nasal before a consonant (పండు paṇḍu, అంటే aṇṭē). *sh* is శ, *ṣ* is ష (in practice both sound like English sh), and జ్ఞ is written *gn*, as it is pronounced. Final *-u* is a real, short, lightly rounded vowel: never swallow it.

pronunciation.title: Short vs long vowels
pronunciation.body:
Telugu distinguishes short and long vowels, and the difference changes meaning: *కలం* (kalam) is a pen, *కాలం* (kālam) is time. A long vowel is held roughly twice as long as a short one; the quality barely changes.

English speakers tend to stretch stressed vowels and shorten unstressed ones. In Telugu, length is fixed by the word, not by stress, so a long vowel stays long wherever it falls (*మామిడి* māmiḍi, mango) and a short vowel stays short.
tips: Clap twice for a long vowel and once for a short one while saying the word.
Don't turn short i and u into the 'uh' of English unstressed syllables.
Watch the vowel sign: ా ీ ూ mark length.

pronunciation.title: Short e/o vs long ē/ō
pronunciation.body:
Unlike Hindi, Telugu has **short e and o** as well as long ē and ō, and they are written with different letters: ఎ/ె vs ఏ/ే, ఒ/ొ vs ఓ/ో. English speakers usually say every e and o long, which turns *మెడ* (meḍa, neck) into *మేడ* (mēḍa, upstairs floor).

Short e is like the e in 'bed', clipped. Short o is like the o in Italian 'otto' or British 'pot' with rounded lips. The long ones are the pure vowels of 'café' and 'go', held, without gliding into 'ee' or 'oo'.
tips: Say short e/o quickly, as if the next consonant cuts them off.
Keep long ē/ō steady; don't let them become 'ey' and 'ow'.
When reading, look for the extra flick that marks the long sign (ే, ో).

pronunciation.title: Retroflex vs dental consonants
pronunciation.body:
Telugu has two sets of t, d, n (and l): **dental** త ద న ల, with the tongue tip pressed against the back of the upper teeth, and **retroflex** ట డ ణ ళ, with the tongue tip curled back to touch the roof of the mouth behind the ridge. English t and d sit in between, so to Telugu ears an English speaker's t sounds retroflex.

The difference matters: *పాట* (pāṭa) is a song, *పాత* (pāta) means old. For dentals, think Spanish or French t; for retroflexes, curl the tongue back and let it flick forward as you release.
tips: For త/ద: put your tongue tip on your teeth, as if about to say 'th', and say t/d.
For ట/డ: curl the tip up and back; the sound becomes hollow and heavy.
English loanwords use retroflex: టీ ṭī tea, డాక్టర్ ḍākṭar doctor.

pronunciation.title: Aspiration (mostly in loanwords)
pronunciation.body:
The aspirated letters ఖ ఘ ఛ ఝ ఠ ఢ థ ధ ఫ భ appear mainly in words borrowed from Sanskrit, Urdu and English. Native Telugu words use the plain consonants.

In careful and educated speech, aspirates are said with a clear puff of air (or breathy voice for gh, dh, bh). In casual speech many speakers weaken them, so *కథ* (katha) can sound like 'kata'. You should aim for the careful pronunciation, but don't be surprised when you hear it reduced. Equally important: plain క ప త are **not** aspirated, unlike English k p t at the start of a word.
tips: Hold a paper strip in front of your mouth: it should flutter for ఖ ఫ థ, stay still for క ప త.
Say 'pat' with no puff of air, like the p in 'spat', for ప.
ఫ in English loanwords is f: ఫోను (fōnu), కాఫీ (kāfī).

pairs.note: Not a strict pair; compare t and th.

pronunciation.title: The retroflex ళ
pronunciation.body:
ళ (ḷa) is an l said with the tongue tip curled back, as for ట and డ. It is extremely common in native words, especially doubled: *నీళ్ళు* (nīḷḷu, water), *కళ్ళు* (kaḷḷu, eyes), *ఇళ్ళు* (iḷḷu, houses), *వాళ్ళు* (vāḷḷu, they).

The plain ల is a clear l with the tongue close to the teeth. Mixing them up can change the meaning (*కల* kala, dream vs *కళ* kaḷa, art) and immediately marks a foreign accent. Note that the spelling ళ్ళ is often printed as ళ్ల; both are pronounced ḷḷ.
tips: Say 'll' with your tongue curled back until the tip touches the roof of your mouth.
Practise ల–ళ in alternation: la–ḷa–la–ḷa.
Doubled ళ్ళ is held: kaḷ-ḷu.

pronunciation.title: Double consonants (gemination)
pronunciation.body:
A doubled consonant in Telugu is genuinely **held longer**, the way Italians say 'pizza' or English 'bookcase' joins two k's. *పతి* (pati, husband) and *పత్తి* (patti, cotton) differ only in that hold.

Gemination is everywhere in basic vocabulary: *అమ్మ* amma, *అక్క* akka, *అన్న* anna, *కొత్త* kotta, *ఇల్లు* illu. If you say these with a single consonant you will sound clipped or be misunderstood. For stops, close the mouth, pause a beat, then release.
tips: Pause briefly with the closure held: kot–ta, not ko-ta.
The vowel before a double consonant stays short.
The spelling tells you: a vottu of the same letter (క్క, త్త, ల్ల) means double.

pairs.note: Not a strict pair; compare the held d.

pronunciation.title: Nasals and the sunna (ం)
pronunciation.body:
The circle ం (*sunna*) stands for a nasal consonant. At the **end of a word** it is pronounced *m*: *పుస్తకం* pustakam, *నమస్కారం* namaskāram. **Before a consonant** it takes the position of that consonant: before క/గ it is ṅ (*రంగు* raṅgu, colour), before చ/జ ñ (*మంచి* manchi, good), before ట/డ ṇ (*పండు* paṇḍu, fruit), before త/ద n (*అందం* andam, beauty), before ప/బ m (*సంబరం* sambaram, celebration).

Telugu also has the full nasal letters న, మ, ణ, and rare ఙ, ఞ. Telugu has no nasalised vowels like Hindi's; ం is always a real consonant. Words ending in ం often drop the final m colloquially before adding endings: *పుస్తకం* + *లో* = *పుస్తకంలో* (pustakamlō).
tips: Don't nasalise the vowel; close your mouth or touch the tongue for a real m/n.
Before ప/బ, close your lips: సంపద sampada.
Final -am words are very common nouns (Sanskrit-origin).

pairs.note: Dental n vs retroflex ṇ, both written with ం.

pronunciation.title: The final -u
pronunciation.body:
A huge number of Telugu words end in a short **-u**: *ఇల్లు* illu, *పాలు* pālu, *నేను* nēnu, *రెండు* reṇḍu. This -u is a real vowel, short and with only slight lip rounding; in fast speech it can sound close to the 'u' in 'put' or even a very short 'ŭ'. It must not disappear: *పాలు* is not 'pāl'.

The -u often changes when suffixes are added. Many nouns switch to -i or to a special *oblique* stem: *ఇల్లు* (house) → *ఇంటికి* (to the house), *ఊరు* (town) → *ఊరికి* (to the town), *కాలు* (leg) → *కాలికి* (to the leg). Plurals add *-lu*: *పుస్తకాలు* (books). Learn the oblique stem together with the noun.
tips: End the word with a light, short u, as in 'put', not a long 'oo'.
Masculine nouns and verbs often end -ḍu: వాడు, అన్నయ్య వచ్చాడు.
Before -lō/-ki, check the stem: ఇల్లు → ఇంట్లో, ఊరు → ఊళ్ళో.

pronunciation.title: Telugu words end in vowels
pronunciation.body:
Native Telugu words almost always end in a vowel, which gives the language its flowing, 'Italian' rhythm. Borrowed words that end in a consonant are traditionally given a vowel, usually -u: *బస్* → *బస్సు* (bassu, bus), *కార్* → *కారు* (kāru, car), *రూమ్* → *రూము* (rūmu, room), *టికెట్* → *టికెట్టు* (ṭikeṭṭu). Note that a final consonant often doubles before the added -u.

In modern urban speech and writing, English words are also used as-is with the pollu (*ఫోన్*, *బస్*), but adding the vowel is what you will hear in most of the state and what makes case endings easy: *బస్సులో* (bassulō, in the bus).
tips: When you borrow an English word, try adding -u: 'pen' → పెన్ను pennu.
Short vowels in the middle of words are never dropped as in Hindi: మనిషి is ma-ni-ṣi.
Link words smoothly; Telugu flows vowel to consonant to vowel.

pronunciation.title: చ and జ: ch/j or ts/dz?
pronunciation.body:
Telugu చ and జ have two pronunciations. Before front vowels (i, ī, e, ē) and in Sanskrit or English loans they are like English *ch* and *j*: *చేప* chēpa (fish), *జీతం* jītam (salary). In many native words before a, ā, o, ō, u, especially in coastal Andhra speech, they are said as **ts** and **dz**: *చాలా* tsālā (very), *చూడు* tsūḍu (look), *జారు* dzāru (slip).

The script used to have separate letters for ts and dz (ౘ, ౙ), but these are now obsolete. Speakers in Telangana and many urban speakers use ch/j throughout, so both are acceptable; this course writes ch and j everywhere.
tips: Saying ch/j everywhere is always understood and sounds standard in Hyderabad.
For a coastal sound, try ts in చాలా (tsālā) and చూడు (tsūḍu), but keep ch in చెప్పు (front vowel e).
Listen to film dialogue: older and coastal speakers use ts/dz more.

pronunciation.title: Historic letters: ఱ, ఁ and old spellings
pronunciation.body:
Older Telugu distinguished a 'hard' r, ఱ (*bandi ra*), from the ordinary ర, and marked a half-nasal with ఁ (*arasunna*). In the modern language both distinctions are gone: ఱ is pronounced exactly like ర and ఁ is silent. School textbooks still teach them and you will meet them in classical poetry, old books and some formal names.

Modern spelling simply writes ర and drops ఁ: *ఱెక్క* → *రెక్క* (rekka, wing), *వాఁడు* → *వాడు* (vāḍu, he). When you see them, just read ర and ignore ఁ.
tips: Read ఱ as an ordinary tapped r.
Ignore ఁ when reading aloud.
You never need to write these yourself.

pronunciation.title: Spoken vs written: common contractions
pronunciation.body:
Everyday spoken Telugu shortens many written forms, and these are what you will hear in films and on the street. The most important: the first-person verb ending *-ānu* is shortened to *-ā*: *వస్తాను* (vastānu) → *వస్తా* (vastā), *ఉన్నాను* (unnānu) → *ఉన్నా* (unnā). *ఏమిటి* (ēmiṭi, what) becomes *ఏంటి* (ēṇṭi); *ఎలా ఉన్నారు* (elā unnāru) is run together as *ఎలా ఉన్నారు* → 'elunnāru'; the continuous *చేస్తున్నది* is *చేస్తోంది* (chēstōndi).

Words also run together: *ఏమి + ఉంది* → *ఏముంది* (ēmundi, what is there), *బాగా + ఉన్నారా* → *బాగున్నారా* (bāgunnārā). Learn the full form so you can read, and the short form so you can follow conversations.
tips: In speech, -ānu → -ā is normal and not rude: వస్తా, చెప్తా, చూస్తా.
ఏంటి is the everyday 'what'; ఏమిటి is careful or written.
Vowels at word boundaries merge: అది + ఏమిటి → అదేమిటి.

pronunciation.title: Stress, rhythm and question intonation
pronunciation.body:
Telugu stress is light and usually falls on the **first syllable**; it never shortens other vowels as English stress does. Every syllable gets its full vowel, so the rhythm is even and 'syllable-timed'. Long vowels and double consonants, not stress, give a word its shape.

Yes/no questions are formed by adding **-ā** to the last word, with a rise on it: *వస్తారు* (they come) → *వస్తారా?* (vastārā?, will you come?). Question-word questions (*ఎక్కడ*, *ఏమిటి*) have a falling tone. The tag *కదా* (kadā, isn't it?) seeks agreement, and the particle *-ē* adds emphasis: *నేనే* (nēnē, it's me myself).
tips: Don't swallow unstressed vowels: pustakam, not 'pust-kum'.
Rise on the final -ā of a yes/no question.
Use కదా? like 'right?' at the end of a sentence.

a.en: they will come / you will come
